The DOORS are attested reading-traditions surfaced from the retrieved reception (Catena Aurea, Newman tr.), NOT authored from recall; each witness summary is grounded in the actual Catena text on this pericope. The editorial framing (gravity/trap/hinge/say/do) is AI-drafted and pending Wilson's curation. Choosing one door = rejecting the others; that act of focus is the point. [v2 migration 2026-09-10: gravity/synthesis moved under tracks.complementary (verified against that track's first reading, not assumed); the other track has firstReading only, pending Phase 4b authoring.] [Phase 4b 2026-09-10, Opus: Gospel doors gained Glossa (Migne 22:8, 22:11) witnesses; semicontinuous half authored — gravity, synthesis, two Exodus 32 doors — from src/turn_pull.py output.]
trap: The text collapses into a dress code: "make sure you're wearing the right thing," and free grace turns into anxious self-policing. The opposite trap is just as easy — "everyone's invited!" — which waves the garment away and loses the King's hard question. Both dissolve the tension the parable refuses to drop.
hinge: The invitation could not be freer — it runs past the worthy to the bad and good alike in the streets — and the King still throws out the man with no garment. Free grace that nonetheless expects you to be changed. You cannot preach this text by dropping either half.

doors.claim: Grace seats you at the table and then asks you to wear it — the feast is free, but it is not indifferent to who you become.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: The wedding garment is charity — the love the Lord himself wore when he came to wed the Church to himself. To sit at the feast without it is to be present and still not dressed.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The wedding garment is the righteousness of Christ, first imputed, then implanted — given to us, then growing in us.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: He goes to the feast without a garment who goes seeking his own honour and not the Bridegroom's.

doors.say: You are welcome here, and welcome is not the end of it — put on the love you were given.
doors.do: Send them to examine one place this week where they have come to the table seeking their own honour, and to put on Christ there instead.

doors.landing: The invitation ran to the streets
doors.claim: The ones first asked would not come, so the doors were thrown open to the crossings of the road — and that is where we were standing.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The first servant sent is Moses, then the Prophets, to those already invited; and the Gentiles were not even in the streets but out in the crossings of the streets, gathered in last.

witnesses.author: Remigius of Auxerre
witnesses.reading: Those first bidden — the people who thought the feast was theirs — were found not worthy, and the hall was filled from the roads instead.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: To the outgoings: actions are the ways, the outgoings are the failing of actions, because for the most part those are easily converted whom no prosperity attends in earthly doings.

doors.say: This feast reached you because grace refuses an empty hall — you are the unlikely guest, gathered from the crossroads.
doors.do: Move them from astonishment at being included to widening the table — naming who is still out in the crossings of their own town.

doors.landing: A hall of bad and good
doors.claim: The wedding hall this side of the end holds bad with good together, and the garment-inspection belongs to the King, not to the guests.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: By the wedding-feast is meant the present Church, into which some enter who shall yet perish; in this present Church there cannot be bad without good, nor good without bad — and he is not good who refuses to endure the bad.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: The marriage-feast is filled when those gathered by the Apostles sit down — but it behoved that both bad and good be gathered in, until the King himself comes in to see the guests.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He adds that not all who are in the Church are worthy of the kingdom, lest his own grow slothful.

doors.say: You are sitting in a mixed hall, and your job is not to inspect your neighbour's garment but to wear your own and trust the King to sort the feast.
doors.do: Turn them from policing the hall to patient love within it — one concrete way to "endure the bad" without leaving the table.

complementary.gravity: The day stacks toward one image and one threat. Isaiah's feast on the mountain where death is swallowed up, the table prepared in Psalm 23, and a wedding hall thrown open to the streets — and then, at the very edge of the joy, a guest with no garment and a door shut fast. Grace is a feast freely given, and it lays a claim on the one who comes.

synthesis.convergence: Three tables and a swallowed death: the feast God spreads on the mountain where the shroud over the peoples is destroyed (Isaiah 25), the table prepared in the valley's shadow (Psalm 23), the wedding hall thrown open to the streets (Matthew 22) — with Paul's charge to rejoice and stop being anxious. The banquet of grace is set and free, and it still lays a claim on the one who comes.
synthesis.claim: The table is set, death is swallowed up, and you are invited — so come, and come clothed.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that knows grief — the shroud is real to them — and tends toward either anxious self-policing or a welcome too cheap to change anyone, the move is to seat them at the freely-set table and then let the wedding garment ask what life the feast is calling them to put on.

doors.claim: The calf is born of impatience: a God who stays with them is not enough, they want one they can see going before them, and they slide there by small steps.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: They were weary of waiting for the promised land. They thought themselves detained too long at Mount Sinai. They had a God that stayed with them, but they must have a God to go before them.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Eating and drinking drove them to play, and play to idolatry. He that despises little things, falls little by little.

doors.say: They didn't set out to abandon God. They just got tired of waiting, and wanted something they could hold.
doors.do: Ask them to name what they reach for when God seems slow, and to bring that impatience to prayer instead.

doors.claim: God's "let me alone" turns out to be an opening for prayer, and Moses takes it: one person's intercession stands between a people and ruin.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Now Moses is standing in the gap to turn away the wrath of God. He took the hint which God gave him when he said, Let me alone, which, though it seemed to forbid his interceding, did really encourage it, by shewing what power the prayer of faith hath with God.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: See here, the power of prayer, God suffers himself to be prevailed with by humble believing importunity.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He brings in the fathers, who are loved, on behalf of the sons, who offend, and do not deserve to be heard.

doors.say: God said, "leave me alone." Moses heard an invitation, and he stayed and prayed.
doors.do: Have them choose one person or community who has gone astray and stand in the breach for them in prayer every day this week.

semicontinuous.gravity: Tired of waiting for Moses, Israel melts its gold into a calf and holds a feast to it at the foot of the mountain where the law was given; God says "let me alone," and Moses will not, standing in the breach until the Lord relents (Exodus 32). The Psalm remembers the calf in Horeb and Moses in the breach; Paul answers anxiety with prayer (Philippians 4); and the king's invited guests refuse his wedding feast. The nerve: we trade God's feast for one we can make and hold, and someone must stand in the gap.

synthesis.convergence: Impatient Israel builds a god it can see and feasts before it, while Moses stands between the people and destruction (Exodus 32); the Psalm remembers the calf and the one who stood in the breach (Psalm 106); Paul meets anxiety with prayer and thanksgiving (Philippians 4); and the invited guests choose their farms and their trade over the king's feast (Matthew 22). Each reading shows people trading God's feast for something of their own making, and a grace that keeps interceding and inviting anyway.
synthesis.claim: When waiting wears us down we build something we can hold instead of God; the answer is someone standing in the gap, and a feast still open.
synthesis.here: For people whose impatience with God has drifted into trust in what they can control — money, plans, leaders — the move is Moses' prayer: stand in the breach for others, and come back to the table.

subtract: These three are doors, not points — mutually exclusive landings (a changed life / astonished welcome / patient humility). Walk through one and let the other two go; the choosing is the sermon's focus.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
